query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an unmodified α + β dual-phase alloy whose low hardness and poor friction and wear properties limit its use under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could improve its hardness and wear resistance without sacrificing its existing beneficial properties. State the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, applicable operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A two‐stage low‐temperature plasma oxy‐nitriding treatment immediately followed by a controlled laser surface texturing process will improve the surface hardness and wear resistance of TC4 without degrading its inherent ductility and corrosion performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Unmodified TC4 (Ti6Al4V) dual‐phase alloy having relatively low surface hardness and suboptimal wear resistance while remaining attractive for its corrosion resistance and biocompatibility.
generation.intervention: First, subject TC4 to a low‐temperature (≤650–700 °C) plasma oxy‐nitriding process in two stages: an oxygen‐rich first step to disrupt continuous TiN barrier formation, followed by a nitrogen‐rich step to promote deeper diffusion of N (and residual O) into the substrate. Second, perform a brief laser surface texturing with parameters tuned to minimally perturb the modified layer.
generation.conditions: Processing temperatures remain below 700 °C to avoid detrimental phase transformations; the laser texturing parameters (pulse energy, scanning speed) are adjusted to form shallow, uniform micro-reservoirs without inducing excessive roughness or microcracking. Testing should be under dry sliding conditions and moderate to high contact stresses typical of extreme-service applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A gradient, discontinuous compound layer containing hard Ti–N and Ti–O/N phases coupled with an inter-connected porous substructure forms in the near-surface region; the superimposed microtexturing further refines the topography, reducing contact area and local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: The initial oxy‐nitriding stage uses oxygen to break up a continuous TiN layer—thereby allowing deeper and more uniform nitrogen (and oxygen) penetration—resulting in a hardened yet ductile diffusion layer. The subsequent laser texturing creates micro-reservoirs that capture wear debris and reduce friction by lowering the effective contact area, reinforcing the wear resistance without compromising the favorable properties of the bulk alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with untreated TC4, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit a surface hardness increase by roughly 2–3 times and a substantially reduced wear rate (potentially at least one order of magnitude lower under comparable sliding conditions) while maintaining its corrosion resistance and ductility.
generation.baseline: Performance characteristics and tribological behavior of untreated TC4 alloy under identical test loads and conditions.
generation.boundary: Treatment effects are expected to hold provided that the process temperature is maintained below 700 °C and that the laser texturing is precisely controlled to avoid excessive surface damage; the improvements are specifically anticipated for applications subjected to high contact stresses in dry or lightly lubricated environments.
generation.uncertainty: While separate studies (PMC10222207 and PMC11396705) support improved wear resistance from low-temperature plasma nitriding/oxy-nitriding and laser texturing respectively, the combined effect—especially at the reduced temperatures that preserve TC4’s intrinsic beneficial properties—is less established. The interaction between the porous, oxygen-boosted diffusion layer and the laser-induced microtexturing in achieving an optimal balance of hardness and toughness is the novel aspect that needs further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of TC4 samples: one undergoing the two-stage low-temperature plasma oxy-nitriding followed by controlled laser surface texturing, and the other remaining unmodified. Conduct standardized ball-on-disk and sliding wear tests under the same load (e.g., 8 N) and sliding distance (e.g., 1000 m). In parallel, perform microhardness measurements (using Vickers indentation) and detailed microstructural analyses (SEM, XRD) on both sets.
measurements: Wear volume or wear rate (mg or mm³/N·m)
Surface morphology and phase composition before and after wear tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be considered falsified if the treated samples show less than a 1.5-fold increase in surface hardness or do not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., greater than 50%) reduction in wear volume compared to the untreated TC4 under identical test conditions, or if detrimental changes (such as loss of ductility or corrosion resistance indicators) are observed.

cited_evidence.text: Metals, including many kinds of composites, are greatly popular in modern industry [,,,,,,,]. Among them, titanium and its alloys are widely used in aircraft, aerospace, and marine equipment due to their light weight, high specific strength, and excellent corrosion resistance [,,,]. However, they are susceptible to abrasion because of low wear resistance, which is their principal drawback [,]. Therefore, surface-hardening titanium alloys with hardened layers tens to hundreds of microns thick can benefit significantly from the application of a kind of substrate-strengthening thermochemical diffusion treatment: plasma nitriding [,,]. Plasma nitriding favors the formation of hard and wear-resistant ceramic compound layers of titanium nitrides on titanium and its alloys, as well as a solid-solution sublayer of N-interstitial α-Ti crystals []. High-temperature nitriding with a long time of treatment can significantly improve the hardness and wear performance of titanium alloys [,,] but can cause mechanical degradation, unpredictable deformation, and even β phase transformation leading to failure of the industrial components []. The growth of the Ti-N compound layer was enhanced by the use of an NH3-N2 mixture during the plasma nitriding of the Ti6Al4V alloy. After nitriding at 750 °C for 4 h in an NH3-N2 (1:2) atmosphere, a Ti-N compound layer approximately 2 μm thick was formed on the Ti6Al4V alloy. The Ti-N compound layers are typically much harder than the titanium alloy substrate. In comparison to the un-nitrided titanium alloy, samples nitrided in an NH3-N2 mixture exhibited the complete elimination of stick–tear and plowing wear throughout the duration of the test, resulting in undetectable wear loss when in contact with bearing steel. The oxide layer formed on the wear track by the transfer of material from the counterpart steel ball reduced the average friction coefficient from approximately 0.55 to 0.30 under an 8N load. The formation of the Ti-N layer not only enhances the hardness and wear resistance of the titanium alloy but also increases its corrosion resistance.

The previous work shows that the nitrided titanium alloy has a higher hardness, which is of great benefit to improve the service life [], but the brittleness of nitriding layers results in the abrasive wear. Borghi et al. [] studied tribological effects of surface texturing on nitriding steel for high-performance engine applications, and the results show that in “dry contact” configuration, for a normal load of 1N, friction coefficient is reduced to about 10% from untextured to textured surface. However, the effect of surface texturing and nitriding composite treatment on the tribological properties of titanium has not been deeply investigated. In this study, the titanium alloy samples were nitrided at 750, 800, 850, 900, and 950 °C, respectively, for 10 h in a plasma nitriding furnace. Then, surface textures were fabricated on the nitrided samples by laser process system. For comparison, surface textures were also prepared on the polished titanium alloy. The present work aims to study the combined effect of surface textures and nitriding on the tribological performance of titanium alloy.
